title: Αἱ πύλαι ῥηγνύμεναι
titleEn: The Breaking of the Gates — Iliad 12.378–471
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Ajax kills Epicles with a rock from the wall, Teucer wounds Glaucus, who slips away unseen, and Sarpedon kills Alcmaon and tears down a section of battlement, opening a gap. Ajax and Teucer both go for him, but Zeus turns the fatal blow from his son; Sarpedon gives ground a little, then calls to the Lycians to follow him, since a path is easier forced by many. The fight at the wall hangs level, like a working woman’s scales, until Zeus gives the greater glory to Hector. He calls the Trojans on, lifts a huge stone that two men of today could not stir, and hurls it at the doors; the bolts and hinges give way, and he leaps in like night, with fire in his eyes. The Trojans pour over the wall and through the gates, and the Danaans flee among the ships.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δὲ πρῶτος Τελαμώνιος ἄνδρα κατέκτα
Σαρπήδοντος ἑταῖρον Ἐπικλῆα μεγάθυμον
μαρμάρῳ ὀκριόεντι βαλών, ὅ ῥα τείχεος ἐντὸς
κεῖτο μέγας παρ’ ἔπαλξιν ὑπέρτατος·
sentences.tr:
Aias de prōtos Telamōnios andra katekta
Sarpēdontos hetairon Epiklēa megathymon
marmarōi okrioenti balōn, ho rha teicheos entos
keito megas par’ epalxin hypertatos·
sentences.l:
And Ajax first, Telamonian, killed a man,
Sarpedon’s companion, Epicles, great-hearted,
by striking him with a jagged rock, which inside the wall
lay, great, beside the battlement, uppermost;
sentences.i: Telamonian Ajax was the first to kill a man: Epicles, the great-hearted companion of Sarpedon, whom he struck with a jagged rock that lay inside the wall, a great one, uppermost beside the battlement;
sentences.n: Αἴας … Τελαμώνιος is the stock ‘Telamonian Ajax’, split by πρῶτος ‘first’; the epithet tells him from the other Ajax, son of Oileus. κατέκτα is the aorist of κτείνω ‘kill’. ἑταῖρον ‘companion’ and the stock μεγάθυμον ‘great-hearted’ both go with Ἐπικλῆα. μαρμάρῳ ὀκριόεντι is ‘with a jagged rock’ (μάρμαρος is any hard rock, not yet marble), and βαλών is the aorist participle ‘striking’. ὅ is the relative ‘which’, the rock; κεῖτο is ‘lay’, and ὑπέρτατος ‘uppermost’ says it lay on top.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κέ μιν ῥέα
χείρεσσ’ ἀμφοτέρῃς ἔχοι ἀνὴρ οὐδὲ μάλ’ ἡβῶν,
οἷοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσ’·
sentences.tr:
oude ke min rhea
cheiress’ amphoterēis echoi anēr oude mal’ hēbōn,
hoioi nyn brotoi eis’·
sentences.i: and a man could not easily hold it in both hands, not even one fully in youthful prime, such as mortals now are;
sentences.n: μιν is the rock. οὐδέ κε … ἔχοι is a potential optative, ‘could not hold’. ἀμφοτέρῃς is the Homeric feminine dative plural with χείρεσσ’ (for χερσίν), ‘with both hands’. ἡβῶν is the present participle of ἡβάω ‘be in youthful prime’, and μάλ’ strengthens it. οἷοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσ’ is the poet’s stock aside, ‘such as mortals now are’, setting the heroes of the story above the men of his own day; the same words come again at 449.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑψόθεν ἔμβαλ’ ἀείρας,
θλάσσε δὲ τετράφαλον κυνέην, σὺν δ’ ὀστέ’ ἄραξε
πάντ’ ἄμυδις κεφαλῆς·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ar’ hypsothen embal’ aeiras,
thlasse de tetraphalon kyneēn, syn d’ oste’ araxe
pant’ amydis kephalēs·
sentences.i: he lifted it and hurled it in from above, and it smashed the four-ridged helmet and crushed all the bones of the head together;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Ajax, and the rock, it seems, is the subject of θλάσσε and ἄραξε. ἔμβαλ’ is the aorist of ἐμβάλλω ‘throw in’; ἀείρας is ‘lifting’. θλάσσε is the epic aorist of θλάω ‘crush’ (doubled σ), unaugmented. τετράφαλον ‘four-ridged’ is the same kind of helmet as the τετραφάληρον of 5.743; what a φάλος is, and what the four are, is not certain. σὺν … ἄραξε is tmesis, ‘crushed together’ (ἀράσσω ‘smash’), and πάντ’ ἄμυδις ‘all together’ adds that nothing was left whole. κεφαλῆς ‘of the head’ goes with ὀστέ’ (ὀστέα) ‘the bones’. Nearly the same words stand at Odyssey 12.412–413, of the helmsman, with a falling mast for the rock.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀρνευτῆρι ἐοικὼς
κάππεσ’ ἀφ’ ὑψηλοῦ πύργου, λίπε δ’ ὀστέα θυμός.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ar’ arneutēri eoikōs
kappes’ aph’ hypsēlou pyrgou, lipe d’ ostea thymos.
sentences.l:
and he, like a diver,
fell down from the high tower, and left his bones the spirit.
sentences.i: and he, like a diver, tumbled from the high tower, and his spirit left his bones.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Epicles. ἀρνευτῆρι is the dative of ἀρνευτήρ, one who plunges headfirst, a ‘diver’, after ἐοικώς ‘like’. κάππεσ’ is κατέπεσε, with the τ of κατ- assimilated to the following π: ‘fell down’. ἀφ’ ὑψηλοῦ πύργου is ‘from the high tower’. θυμός is the life-spirit and is the subject of λίπε ‘left’; ὀστέα ‘bones’ is its object. The two lines are close to Odyssey 12.413–414, where the helmsman falls from the ship’s decking.

sentences.t:
Τεῦκρος δὲ Γλαῦκον κρατερὸν παῖδ’ Ἱππολόχοιο
ἰῷ ἐπεσσύμενον βάλε τείχεος ὑψηλοῖο,
ᾗ ῥ’ ἴδε γυμνωθέντα βραχίονα, παῦσε δὲ χάρμης.
sentences.tr:
Teukros de Glaukon krateron paid’ Hippolochoio
iōi epessymenon bale teicheos hypsēloio,
hēi rh’ ide gymnōthenta brachiona, pause de charmēs.
sentences.l:
And Teucer Glaucus, strong son of Hippolochus,
with an arrow, as he rushed on, struck, at the high wall,
where he saw the arm laid bare, and made him cease from the joy of battle.
sentences.i: Teucer struck Glaucus, the strong son of Hippolochus, with an arrow as he rushed at the high wall, where he saw his arm left bare, and put an end to his joy of battle.
sentences.n: Τεῦκρος is the subject and Γλαῦκον the object of βάλε, with the stock κρατερόν ‘strong’ and the patronymic παῖδ’ Ἱππολόχοιο ‘son of Hippolochus’. ἰῷ is ‘with an arrow’ (dative of ἰός). ἐπεσσύμενον is a participle of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush at’, and τείχεος ὑψηλοῖο (epic -οιο) is read with it, ‘at the high wall’; it could instead say where Glaucus was struck. ᾗ is ‘where’; ἴδε is the unaugmented aorist ‘saw’. γυμνωθέντα βραχίονα is ‘the arm laid bare’. παῦσε δὲ χάρμης is ‘made him cease from’, with the genitive; χάρμη is the joy of fighting.

sentences.t:
ἂψ δ’ ἀπὸ τείχεος ἆλτο λαθών, ἵνα μή τις Ἀχαιῶν
βλήμενον ἀθρήσειε καὶ εὐχετόῳτ’ ἐπέεσσι.
sentences.tr:
aps d’ apo teicheos alto lathōn, hina mē tis Achaiōn
blēmenon athrēseie kai euchetoōit’ epeessi.
sentences.l:
And back from the wall he leapt, unnoticed, so that no one of the Achaeans
might see him struck and boast over him with words.
sentences.i: He leapt back from the wall without being noticed, so that none of the Achaeans might see him hit and boast over him in words.
sentences.n: ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, and λαθών the aorist participle of λανθάνω, ‘escaping notice’: he left unseen. ἵνα μή … ἀθρήσειε καὶ εὐχετόῳτ’ is a purpose clause with the optative after a past verb. ἀθρήσειε is ‘might see’, from ἀθρέω; βλήμενον is the aorist participle ‘struck’ (epic, for βληθέντα). εὐχετόῳτ’ is εὐχετόῳτο, the optative of εὐχετάομαι ‘boast, vaunt’, with the open (diectatic) ending, as in αἰτιόωνται; ἐπέεσσι is ‘with words’.

sentences.t:
Σαρπήδοντι δ’ ἄχος γένετο Γλαύκου ἀπιόντος
αὐτίκ’ ἐπεί τ’ ἐνόησεν·
sentences.tr:
Sarpēdonti d’ achos geneto Glaukou apiontos
autik’ epei t’ enoēsen·
sentences.l:
And to Sarpedon grief came at Glaucus’ going away,
at once when he noticed;
sentences.i: Sarpedon felt grief as Glaucus went away, as soon as he noticed it;
sentences.n: ἄχος ‘grief’ is the subject of γένετο, with Σαρπήδοντι ‘to Sarpedon’ the one who feels it. Γλαύκου ἀπιόντος is a genitive absolute, ‘Glaucus going away’, from the participle of ἄπειμι. αὐτίκ’ ἐπεί τ’ ἐνόησεν is ‘at once when he noticed’, the subject being Sarpedon and ἐνόησεν the aorist of νοέω.

sentences.t:
ὅμως δ’ οὐ λήθετο χάρμης,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε Θεστορίδην Ἀλκμάονα δουρὶ τυχήσας
νύξ’, ἐκ δ’ ἔσπασεν ἔγχος·
sentences.tr:
homōs d’ ou lētheto charmēs,
all’ ho ge Thestoridēn Alkmaona douri tychēsas
nyx’, ek d’ espasen enchos·
sentences.i: yet he did not forget the joy of battle: he hit Alcmaon, the son of Thestor, with his spear, stabbed him, and pulled the spear out;
sentences.n: ὅμως is ‘all the same’. λήθετο comes from λήθομαι ‘forget’, which takes the genitive (χάρμης). ἀλλ’ ὅ γε is ‘but he’, Sarpedon. Θεστορίδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Thestor’, and Ἀλκμάονα is a second accusative naming him. δουρὶ τυχήσας is ‘having hit with a spear’ (aorist participle of τυγχάνω). νύξ’ is the aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’; ἐκ … ἔσπασεν is tmesis, ‘drew out’ (σπάω). ἔγχος is another word for the spear.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἑσπόμενος πέσε δουρὶ
πρηνής, ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ βράχε τεύχεα ποικίλα χαλκῷ,
sentences.tr:
ho d’ hespomenos pese douri
prēnēs, amphi de hoi brache teuchea poikila chalkōi,
sentences.l:
and he, following the spear, fell
headlong, and around him clashed the armour, intricate with bronze,
sentences.i: and he fell headlong, following the spear, and his armour, intricate with bronze, clashed around him,
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Alcmaon. ἑσπόμενος δουρί is ‘following the spear’ (ἕπομαι takes the dative): as Sarpedon pulled the spear out, the body came after it. πρηνής is ‘headlong, face down’. ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ βράχε is ‘around him clashed’, ἀμφί being an adverb here and οἱ ‘him’. βράχε is the aorist of βράχω ‘clash, crash’, the subject being τεύχεα ‘armour’. ποικίλα χαλκῷ is ‘intricate with bronze’.

sentences.t:
Σαρπηδὼν δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπαλξιν ἑλὼν χερσὶ στιβαρῇσιν
ἕλχ’, ἣ δ’ ἕσπετο πᾶσα διαμπερές, αὐτὰρ ὕπερθε
τεῖχος ἐγυμνώθη, πολέεσσι δὲ θῆκε κέλευθον.
sentences.tr:
Sarpēdōn d’ ar’ epalxin helōn chersi stibarēisin
helch’, hē d’ hespeto pasa diamperes, autar hyperthe
teichos egymnōthē, poleessi de thēke keleuthon.
sentences.l:
and Sarpedon, taking a battlement in his stout hands,
was pulling, and it followed, the whole of it, right through, and above
the wall was laid bare, and for many he made a path.
sentences.i: Sarpedon took hold of a battlement with his stout hands and pulled, and the whole of it came away, and the wall above was left bare, and he made a path for many.
sentences.n: Σαρπηδὼν δ’ ἄρ’ is the subject; ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘take hold of’, with χερσὶ στιβαρῇσιν ‘stout hands’ (epic dative -ῃσιν). ἕλχ’ is ἕλκε, the imperfect of ἕλκω ‘pull’. ἣ is the battlement, ‘it’ (ἣ δ’ is demonstrative, not relative), and ἕσπετο is the second aorist of ἕπομαι ‘followed’; πᾶσα διαμπερές is ‘all of it, right through’. ἐγυμνώθη is the aorist passive of γυμνόω ‘was laid bare’. πολέεσσι is the epic dative plural of πολύς, and θῆκε κέλευθον is ‘made a path’, Sarpedon again.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ Αἴας καὶ Τεῦκρος ὁμαρτήσανθ’ ὃ μὲν ἰῷ
βεβλήκει τελαμῶνα περὶ στήθεσσι φαεινὸν
ἀσπίδος ἀμφιβρότης·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ Aias kai Teukros homartēsanth’ ho men iōi
beblēkei telamōna peri stēthessi phaeinon
aspidos amphibrotēs·
sentences.i: Ajax and Teucer went at him together, and the one had hit with an arrow the shining shield-strap about his chest, on his man-covering shield;
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’, Sarpedon. ὁμαρτήσανθ’ is the aorist participle of ὁμαρτέω, ‘going together’, with Αἴας καὶ Τεῦκρος. ὃ μὲν is ‘the one’, Teucer (who has the bow), and Αἴας δ’ at 404 is the other. βεβλήκει is the pluperfect ‘had struck’. τελαμών is a strap, here the one that carries the shield across the body (the table’s ‘shield-strap’ of 2.388); ἀσπίδος ἀμφιβρότης is ‘of the man-covering shield’ (see 2.389), and φαεινόν is ‘shining’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ Ζεὺς κῆρας ἄμυνε
παιδὸς ἑοῦ, μὴ νηυσὶν ἔπι πρύμνῃσι δαμείη·
sentences.tr:
alla Zeus kēras amyne
paidos heou, mē nēusin epi prymnēisi dameiē·
sentences.l:
but Zeus warded off the death-fates
of his own son, lest at the ships’ sterns he be overcome;
sentences.i: but Zeus kept the fates of death away from his own son, so that he should not be overcome at the ships’ sterns;
sentences.n: Sarpedon is a son of Zeus, as the words παιδὸς ἑοῦ ‘his own son’ say (ἑοῦ is the possessive ὅς, ‘his own’, not the relative). ἄμυνε is the imperfect of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, with κῆρας ‘fates of death’ as object and the genitive ‘from his son’. μὴ … δαμείη is a negative purpose clause, the aorist passive optative of δαμάζω ‘be overcome’, after a past verb. νηυσὶν ἔπι πρύμνῃσι is ‘at the ships’ sterns’, ἔπι standing after its noun.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ ἀσπίδα νύξεν ἐπάλμενος, οὐδὲ διὰ πρὸ
ἤλυθεν ἐγχείη, στυφέλιξε δέ μιν μεμαῶτα.
sentences.tr:
Aias d’ aspida nyxen epalmenos, oude dia pro
ēlythen encheiē, styphelixe de min memaōta.
sentences.l:
and Ajax stabbed the shield, leaping upon him, and not right through
went the spear, and thrust him roughly, eager as he was.
sentences.i: and Ajax stabbed the shield, springing at him, but the spear did not go right through; it shoved him, eager as he was.
sentences.n: ἐπάλμενος is the aorist participle of ἐφάλλομαι ‘spring at’, in its syncopated epic form. νύξεν is the aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’. διὰ πρό is ‘right through’, two adverbs together. ἤλυθεν is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι, with ἐγχείη ‘spear’ as subject. στυφέλιξε is the aorist of στυφελίζω ‘strike hard, thrust’, and μεμαῶτα the perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, agreeing with μιν, Sarpedon. The second line is 7.261 in the duel of Ajax and Hector, where the spear did go through the shield.

sentences.t: χώρησεν δ’ ἄρα τυτθὸν ἐπάλξιος·
sentences.tr: chōrēsen d’ ara tytthon epalxios·
sentences.l: And he withdrew a little from the battlement;
sentences.i: He drew back a little from the battlement;
sentences.n: χώρησεν is the aorist of χωρέω ‘give way, withdraw’, and τυτθόν is ‘a little’. ἐπάλξιος is the genitive singular of ἔπαλξις ‘battlement’, the genitive of separation after the verb of withdrawing: ‘from the battlement’. The subject is still Sarpedon.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὅ γε πάμπαν
χάζετ’, ἐπεί οἱ θυμὸς ἐέλπετο κῦδος ἀρέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ho ge pampan
chazet’, epei hoi thymos eelpeto kydos aresthai.
sentences.l:
but he did not altogether
give ground, since his spirit hoped to win glory.
sentences.i: but he did not give ground altogether, for his spirit hoped to win glory.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὅ γε is ‘but not he’, Sarpedon, and πάμπαν ‘altogether’ goes with χάζετ’, the imperfect of χάζομαι ‘give ground’. ἐέλπετο is the epic imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘hope’; οἱ is ‘his’, with θυμός. ἀρέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἄρνυμαι ‘win’, and κῦδος is ‘glory’.

sentences.t: κέκλετο δ’ ἀντιθέοισιν ἑλιξάμενος Λυκίοισιν·
sentences.tr: kekleto d’ antitheoisin helixamenos Lykioisin·
sentences.l: And he gave orders to the godlike Lycians, turning himself about:
sentences.i: He gave orders to the godlike Lycians, turning round:
sentences.n: κέκλετο is the reduplicated aorist of κέλομαι ‘command, call on’, here with the dative Λυκίοισιν; the table’s ‘gave orders to’ is kept, although what follows is an appeal. ἀντιθέοισιν is the stock epithet ‘godlike’. ἑλιξάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἑλίσσω ‘turn’, ‘turning round’. The speech is Sarpedon’s.

sentences.t: ὦ Λύκιοι τί τ’ ἄρ’ ὧδε μεθίετε θούριδος ἀλκῆς;
sentences.tr: ō Lykioi ti t’ ar’ hōde methiete thouridos alkēs;
sentences.l: “O Lycians, why then do you thus slacken from impetuous might?
sentences.i: “Lycians, why do you slacken like this from your impetuous might?
sentences.n: ὦ Λύκιοι is a vocative. τί τ’ ἄρ’ ὧδε is ‘why then in this way’. μεθίετε is the present of μεθίημι ‘let go, slacken’, here with the genitive, ‘slacken from’; θούριδος ἀλκῆς is ‘impetuous might’, a stock phrase of the Iliad (θοῦρις ‘rushing, impetuous’).

sentences.t:
ἀργαλέον δέ μοί ἐστι καὶ ἰφθίμῳ περ ἐόντι
μούνῳ ῥηξαμένῳ θέσθαι παρὰ νηυσὶ κέλευθον·
sentences.tr:
argaleon de moi esti kai iphthimōi per eonti
mounōi rhēxamenōi thesthai para nēusi keleuthon·
sentences.l:
And hard it is for me, even though I am mighty,
alone, having broken through, to make a path by the ships;
sentences.i: It is hard for me, mighty as I am, to break through alone and make a path by the ships;
sentences.n: ἀργαλέον ‘hard’ takes the infinitive θέσθαι ‘to make’ (aorist middle of τίθημι), with θέσθαι … κέλευθον ‘to make a path’, as θῆκε κέλευθον at 399. ἰφθίμῳ περ ἐόντι is a dative participle agreeing with μοί, ‘even being mighty’, περ making it concessive; ἴφθιμος is the stock ‘mighty’. μούνῳ ‘alone’ agrees with it too. ῥηξαμένῳ is the aorist middle participle of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’: ‘having broken through’, the thing broken (the wall) left unsaid.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐφομαρτεῖτε·
sentences.tr: all’ ephomarteite·
sentences.l: but follow along;
sentences.i: but follow along;
sentences.n: ἐφομαρτεῖτε is the present imperative plural of ἐφομαρτέω ‘go along with, follow close’, contracted from -έετε; the Lycians are told to follow Sarpedon, though he is not named.

sentences.t: πλεόνων δέ τι ἔργον ἄμεινον.
sentences.tr: pleonōn de ti ergon ameinon.
sentences.l: and of more the work is somewhat better.”
sentences.i: the work of a larger number is somewhat better.”
sentences.n: πλεόνων is the genitive plural of the comparative of πολύς, ‘of more’, with ἔργον ‘work’. τι is the small adverbial ‘somewhat’ (it could also be read ‘in any way’), and ἄμεινον ‘better’ is the comparative of ἀγαθός. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δὲ ἄνακτος ὑποδείσαντες ὁμοκλὴν
μᾶλλον ἐπέβρισαν βουληφόρον ἀμφὶ ἄνακτα.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi de anaktos hypodeisantes homoklēn
mallon epebrisan boulēphoron amphi anakta.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they, fearing the rebuke of the lord,
pressed on the harder around the counsel-bearing lord.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they, afraid of their lord’s shouted rebuke, pressed in the harder around the lord who bears counsel.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the usual ‘so he spoke’. ἄνακτος … ἄνακτα is the same man twice, Sarpedon, the second time with the epithet βουληφόρον ‘counsel-bearing’. ὑποδείσαντες is the aorist participle of ὑποδείδω ‘fear’, and ὁμοκλήν is the shouted rebuke. ἐπέβρισαν is the aorist of ἐπιβρίθω ‘press on, bear down’, and μᾶλλον ‘the harder’. ἀμφί stands between the epithet and ἄνακτα.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐκαρτύναντο φάλαγγας
τείχεος ἔντοσθεν, μέγα δέ σφισι φαίνετο ἔργον·
sentences.tr:
Argeioi d’ heterōthen ekartynanto phalangas
teicheos entosthen, mega de sphisi phaineto ergon·
sentences.l:
And the Argives, from the other side, made strong their battle-lines
inside the wall, and great to them appeared the work;
sentences.i: And the Argives on the other side strengthened their battle-lines inside the wall, and it looked a great task to them,
sentences.n: The Argives are the defenders, the Achaeans under another name. ἑτέρωθεν is ‘from the other side’ (suffix -θεν), and ἐκαρτύναντο the aorist middle of καρτύνω ‘make strong’, with φάλαγγας ‘battle-lines’. τείχεος ἔντοσθεν is ‘inside the wall’. σφισι is ‘to them’, φαίνετο ‘appeared’, and ἔργον ‘work’ here means the task of holding the wall. The first line is 11.215 word for word.

sentences.t:
οὔτε γὰρ ἴφθιμοι Λύκιοι Δαναῶν ἐδύναντο
τεῖχος ῥηξάμενοι θέσθαι παρὰ νηυσὶ κέλευθον,
οὔτέ ποτ’ αἰχμηταὶ Δαναοὶ Λυκίους ἐδύναντο
τείχεος ἂψ ὤσασθαι, ἐπεὶ τὰ πρῶτα πέλασθεν.
sentences.tr:
oute gar iphthimoi Lykioi Danaōn edynanto
teichos rhēxamenoi thesthai para nēusi keleuthon,
oute pot’ aichmētai Danaoi Lykious edynanto
teicheos aps ōsasthai, epei ta prōta pelasthen.
sentences.l:
for neither could the mighty Lycians, the Danaans’
wall having broken, make a path by the ships,
nor ever could the spearmen Danaans the Lycians
thrust back from the wall, since first they had come near.
sentences.i: for the mighty Lycians could not break the Danaans’ wall and make a path by the ships, nor could the Danaan spearmen ever push the Lycians back from the wall, once the two sides had first come near.
sentences.n: οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’, and ἐδύναντο is the imperfect of δύναμαι ‘be able’, taking the infinitives θέσθαι and ὤσασθαι. Δαναῶν goes with τεῖχος, ‘the wall of the Danaans’, although the two words are apart. ῥηξάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ῥήγνυμι, and θέσθαι … κέλευθον repeats the words of 411. αἰχμηταί is ‘spearmen’. ὤσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ὠθέω ‘push’, with ἂψ ‘back’. ἐπεὶ τὰ πρῶτα is ‘since first’, and πέλασθεν is the aorist passive of πελάζω, ‘came near’; the subject is the two armies.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὥς τ’ ἀμφ’ οὔροισι δύ’ ἀνέρε δηριάασθον
μέτρ’ ἐν χερσὶν ἔχοντες ἐπιξύνῳ ἐν ἀρούρῃ,
ὥ τ’ ὀλίγῳ ἐνὶ χώρῳ ἐρίζητον περὶ ἴσης,
ὣς ἄρα τοὺς διέεργον ἐπάλξιες·
sentences.tr:
all’ hōs t’ amph’ ouroisi dy’ anere dēriaasthon
metr’ en chersin echontes epixynōi en arourēi,
hō t’ oligōi eni chōrōi erizēton peri isēs,
hōs ara tous dieergon epalxies·
sentences.l:
But as over boundary-marks two men dispute,
holding measures in their hands, in a common plough-land,
who in a small space quarrel over an equal share,
so then those men the battlements kept apart;
sentences.i: But as two men quarrel over boundary-marks, with measures in their hands, on a plough-land they share, and in a small space dispute over an equal share, so the battlements kept those men apart;
sentences.n: A simile: ἀλλ’ ὥς τ’ … ὣς ἄρα is ‘but as … so’. δύ’ ἀνέρε is the dual ‘two men’, and δηριάασθον, ἐρίζητον are dual verbs; ὥ is the dual relative ‘who’. οὔροισι is the epic dative plural of οὖρος ‘boundary-mark’ (ἀμφί ‘over’). μέτρα are ‘measures’, probably measuring rods; the Greek does not say. ἐπιξύνῳ ‘common, shared’ goes with ἀρούρῃ ‘plough-land’. περὶ ἴσης is ‘over an equal share’. διέεργον is the imperfect of διείργω ‘keep apart’, ἐπάλξιες ‘battlements’ its subject.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὑπὲρ αὐτέων
δῄουν ἀλλήλων ἀμφὶ στήθεσσι βοείας
ἀσπίδας εὐκύκλους λαισήϊά τε πτερόεντα.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hyper auteōn
dēioun allēlōn amphi stēthessi boeias
aspidas eukyklous laisēïa te pteroenta.
sentences.l:
but they, above them,
were hacking at one another’s chests the ox-hide
shields, well-rounded, and the light shields, winged.
sentences.i: and above them they hacked at the ox-hide, well-rounded shields on one another’s chests, and at the winged light shields.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the fighters, and ὑπὲρ αὐτέων is ‘above them’, αὐτέων being the epic genitive plural feminine, for the battlements. δῄουν is the imperfect of δηϊόω ‘hack at’. βοείας ‘ox-hide’ and εὐκύκλους ‘well-rounded’ go with ἀσπίδας; λαισήϊα are light shields. πτερόεντα ‘winged’ is the stock word of ‘winged words’; why it is said of shields is not known. The last two lines are 5.452–453.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δ’ οὐτάζοντο κατὰ χρόα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ,
ἠμὲν ὅτεῳ στρεφθέντι μετάφρενα γυμνωθείη
μαρναμένων, πολλοὶ δὲ διαμπερὲς ἀσπίδος αὐτῆς.
sentences.tr:
polloi d’ outazonto kata chroa nēleï chalkōi,
ēmen hoteōi strephthenti metaphrena gymnōtheiē
marnamenōn, polloi de diamperes aspidos autēs.
sentences.l:
And many were wounded in the flesh with pitiless bronze,
both whoever, once turned, had his back laid bare,
of men fighting, and many right through the shield itself.
sentences.i: Many were wounded in the flesh by pitiless bronze, both fighters who turned and had their backs laid bare, and many right through the shield itself.
sentences.n: οὐτάζοντο is the imperfect passive of οὐτάζω ‘wound’, and κατὰ χρόα is ‘in the flesh’. νηλέϊ χαλκῷ is the stock ‘pitiless bronze’. ἠμὲν ὅτεῳ opens a ‘both … and’ that never gets its ἠδέ; πολλοὶ δέ takes its place. ὅτεῳ is the epic dative of ὅστις, ‘whoever’, with στρεφθέντι the aorist passive participle ‘having turned’; γυμνωθείη is the optative of the general, repeated case, ‘had laid bare’. μαρναμένων is the genitive plural ‘of those fighting’. διαμπερὲς ἀσπίδος αὐτῆς is ‘right through the shield itself’.

sentences.t:
πάντῃ δὴ πύργοι καὶ ἐπάλξιες αἵματι φωτῶν
ἐρράδατ’ ἀμφοτέρωθεν ἀπὸ Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
pantēi dē pyrgoi kai epalxies haimati phōtōn
erradat’ amphoterōthen apo Trōōn kai Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
Everywhere indeed the towers and battlements with the blood of men
were spattered, on both sides, from Trojans and Achaeans.
sentences.i: Everywhere the towers and battlements were spattered with men’s blood, on both sides, from Trojans and Achaeans.
sentences.n: πάντῃ is ‘everywhere’ and δή ‘indeed’. ἐρράδατ’ is ἐρράδαται, the perfect passive of ῥαίνω ‘sprinkle’ (third plural in -αται), with the dative αἵματι ‘with blood’. φωτῶν is the genitive plural of φώς ‘man’. ἀμφοτέρωθεν ἀπὸ Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν is ‘from both sides, from Trojans and Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς ἐδύναντο φόβον ποιῆσαι Ἀχαιῶν,
ἀλλ’ ἔχον ὥς τε τάλαντα γυνὴ χερνῆτις ἀληθής,
ἥ τε σταθμὸν ἔχουσα καὶ εἴριον ἀμφὶς ἀνέλκει
ἰσάζουσ’, ἵνα παισὶν ἀεικέα μισθὸν ἄρηται·
sentences.tr:
all’ oud’ hōs edynanto phobon poiēsai Achaiōn,
all’ echon hōs te talanta gynē chernētis alēthēs,
hē te stathmon echousa kai eirion amphis anelkei
isazous’, hina paisin aeikea misthon arētai·
sentences.l:
But not even so could they cause flight of the Achaeans,
but they held on, as a woman, an honest worker with her hands, holds scales,
who, holding the weight and the wool, lifts them up on either side,
making them level, so that for her children she may win an unseemly wage;
sentences.i: But even so they could not put the Achaeans to flight; they held on, as an honest woman who works with her hands holds scales, holding the weight and the wool and lifting them on either side, making them level, so that she may win an unseemly wage for her children;
sentences.n: φόβος here is ‘flight, rout’, not fear. ἔχον is the imperfect ‘they held’; no object is given, and the sense is that they kept the fight even, as the simile says. χερνῆτις is a woman who earns with her hands, a wool-worker, and ἀληθής is ‘honest’, one who does not cheat the scales. τάλαντα are ‘scales’. ἔχουσα is ‘holding’, and σταθμόν is ‘weight’ (it may also be the beam of the balance; the Greek is not clear), and εἴριον is ‘wool’. ἀμφὶς ἀνέλκει is ‘lifts up on both sides’, and ἰσάζουσ’ ‘making level’. ἄρηται is the aorist subjunctive middle of ἄρνυμαι ‘win’, as ἀρέσθαι at 407. ἀεικέα is ‘unseemly’: a wage too small to be fitting.

sentences.t:
ὣς μὲν τῶν ἐπὶ ἶσα μάχη τέτατο πτόλεμός τε,
πρίν γ’ ὅτε δὴ Ζεὺς κῦδος ὑπέρτερον Ἕκτορι δῶκε
Πριαμίδῃ, ὃς πρῶτος ἐσήλατο τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
hōs men tōn epi isa machē tetato ptolemos te,
prin g’ hote dē Zeus kydos hyperteron Hektori dōke
Priamidēi, hos prōtos esēlato teichos Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
so of them equally the fighting was stretched, and the war,
until indeed Zeus gave greater glory to Hector,
Priam’s-son, who first leapt in at the wall of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: so the fighting and the war were stretched out evenly between them, until Zeus gave greater glory to Hector, son of Priam, who was the first to leap in at the Achaeans’ wall.
sentences.n: τῶν ἐπὶ ἶσα is ‘on equal terms for them’. τέτατο is the pluperfect passive of τείνω ‘was stretched’, with μάχη and πτόλεμος, the epic form of πόλεμος ‘war’, as subjects. πρίν γ’ ὅτε δή is ‘until the time when’. κῦδος ὑπέρτερον is ‘greater glory’. Πριαμίδῃ is ‘Priam’s-son’ in the dative, beside Ἕκτορι. ἐσήλατο is the aorist of ἐσάλλομαι ‘leap in’, with τεῖχος as object; the leap itself is told from 462.

sentences.t: ἤϋσεν δὲ διαπρύσιον Τρώεσσι γεγωνώς·
sentences.tr: ēÿsen de diaprysion Trōessi gegōnōs·
sentences.l: And he shouted piercingly, calling aloud to the Trojans:
sentences.i: And he shouted piercingly, calling aloud to the Trojans:
sentences.n: ἤϋσεν is the aorist of ἀΰω ‘shout’ (the diaeresis is the edition’s). διαπρύσιον is an adverb, ‘piercingly’. γεγωνώς is the perfect participle of γέγωνα ‘call aloud’, with Τρώεσσι ‘to the Trojans’. The speech that follows is Hector’s.

sentences.t:
ὄρνυσθ’ ἱππόδαμοι Τρῶες, ῥήγνυσθε δὲ τεῖχος
Ἀργείων καὶ νηυσὶν ἐνίετε θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ.
sentences.tr:
ornysth’ hippodamoi Trōes, rhēgnysthe de teichos
Argeiōn kai nēusin eniete thespidaes pyr.
sentences.l:
“Rouse yourselves, horse-taming Trojans, and break the wall
of the Argives, and cast upon the ships wondrous-blazing fire.”
sentences.i: “Rouse yourselves, Trojans, tamers of horses, and break through the wall of the Argives, and throw wondrous-blazing fire on the ships.”
sentences.n: ὄρνυσθ’ is the present imperative middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘rouse yourselves’. ἱππόδαμοι is the stock ‘horse-taming’. ῥήγνυσθε is the imperative middle of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’. Ἀργείων is the Achaeans again, here Hector’s name for the enemy. ἐνίετε is the present imperative of ἐνίημι ‘send in, throw on’, with νηυσίν ‘on the ships’. θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ is ‘wondrous-blazing fire’ (θέσπις ‘wondrous’, δαίω ‘blaze’).

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτ’ ἐποτρύνων, οἳ δ’ οὔασι πάντες ἄκουον,
ἴθυσαν δ’ ἐπὶ τεῖχος ἀολλέες·
sentences.tr:
hōs phat’ epotrynōn, hoi d’ ouasi pantes akouon,
ithysan d’ epi teichos aollees·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, urging them on, and they all with their ears listened,
and rushed straight at the wall, all together;
sentences.i: So he spoke to urge them on, and they all listened with their ears and rushed straight at the wall in a body;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (φάτο). ἐποτρύνων is ‘urging on’. οὔασι ἄκουον is ‘heard with their ears’, the plain Homeric way of saying it; οὔασι is the epic dative plural of οὖς. ἴθυσαν is the aorist of ἰθύω ‘rush straight’, and ἀολλέες ‘massed together’.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἔπειτα
κροσσάων ἐπέβαινον ἀκαχμένα δούρατ’ ἔχοντες,
sentences.tr:
hoi men epeita
krossaōn epebainon akachmena dourat’ echontes,
sentences.l:
and some then
were mounting the stepped ledges, holding pointed spears,
sentences.i: some of them climbed on the stepped ledges, holding pointed spears,
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν ἔπειτα is ‘some then’, answered by Ἕκτωρ δ’ in the next unit. κροσσάων is the epic genitive plural of κρόσσαι, a rare word for the stepped, projecting parts of the towers; what exactly they are is not certain. ἐπέβαινον is the imperfect of ἐπιβαίνω ‘step on’, with the genitive. ἀκαχμένα is a perfect participle meaning ‘pointed’ (from the root of ἀκ- ‘sharp’), agreeing with δούρατ’, the neuter plural of δόρυ ‘spear’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἁρπάξας λᾶαν φέρεν, ὅς ῥα πυλάων
ἑστήκει πρόσθε πρυμνὸς παχύς, αὐτὰρ ὕπερθεν
ὀξὺς ἔην·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr d’ harpaxas laan pheren, hos rha pylaōn
hestēkei prosthe prymnos pachys, autar hyperthen
oxys eēn·
sentences.i: Hector snatched up and carried a stone that had stood before the gates, thick at its base but sharp above;
sentences.n: ἁρπάξας is the aorist participle of ἁρπάζω ‘snatch up’, and φέρεν is the unaugmented imperfect ‘carried’. λᾶαν is the accusative of λᾶας ‘stone’. ὅς ῥα is ‘which’; ἑστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, ‘had stood’, with πυλάων (genitive plural) after πρόσθε ‘in front of’. πρυμνός is ‘at the base’ (the same word as πρυμνή ‘stern’), παχύς ‘thick’, ὀξύς ‘sharp’, and ἔην is ἦν.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οὔ κε δύ’ ἀνέρε δήμου ἀρίστω
ῥηϊδίως ἐπ’ ἄμαξαν ἀπ’ οὔδεος ὀχλίσσειαν,
οἷοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσ’·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ou ke dy’ anere dēmou aristō
rhēïdiōs ep’ amaxan ap’ oudeos ochlisseian,
hoioi nyn brotoi eis’·
sentences.i: two men, the best of the people, could not easily heave it from the ground onto a wagon, such as mortals now are;
sentences.n: τὸν is the stone. οὔ κε … ὀχλίσσειαν is a potential optative, ‘could not heave’, from ὀχλίζω ‘heave up with a lever’ (σσ is the epic spelling); its plural verb has the dual subject δύ’ ἀνέρε … ἀρίστω ‘two best men’, with δήμου ‘of the people’. ῥηϊδίως is ‘easily’. ἄμαξα is a wagon, and οὔδεος the genitive of οὖδας ‘ground’. οἷοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσ’ repeats 383.

sentences.t: ὃ δέ μιν ῥέα πάλλε καὶ οἶος.
sentences.tr: ho de min rhea palle kai oios.
sentences.l: but he easily swung it, and alone.
sentences.i: but he swung it easily, even alone.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘but he’ is Hector, and μιν the stone. ῥέα is ‘easily’, πάλλε the imperfect of πάλλω ‘swing’, and οἶος ‘alone’. The words end 5.304, there of Diomedes.

sentences.t: τόν οἱ ἐλαφρὸν ἔθηκε Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω.
sentences.tr: ton hoi elaphron ethēke Kronou païs ankylomēteō.
sentences.l: That for him light made the son of Cronus of crooked cunning.
sentences.i: The son of Cronus of crooked cunning made it light for him.
sentences.n: τόν is ‘it’, the stone, and οἱ ‘for him’. ἐλαφρόν ‘light’ is the object’s complement, and ἔθηκε is ‘made’. Κρόνου πάϊς is ‘son of Cronus’, Zeus, with ἀγκυλομήτεω (epic genitive, for -ου) agreeing with Κρόνου; the meaning of ἀγκυλομήτης is ‘of crooked cunning’, ἀγκύλος ‘curved’ with μῆτις, and its exact sense is not known.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε ποιμὴν ῥεῖα φέρει πόκον ἄρσενος οἰὸς
χειρὶ λαβὼν ἑτέρῃ, ὀλίγον τέ μιν ἄχθος ἐπείγει,
ὣς Ἕκτωρ ἰθὺς σανίδων φέρε λᾶαν ἀείρας,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote poimēn rheia pherei pokon arsenos oios
cheiri labōn heterēi, oligon te min achthos epeigei,
hōs Hektōr ithys sanidōn phere laan aeiras,
sentences.l:
And as when a shepherd easily carries the fleece of a male sheep,
taking it in one hand, and little the burden presses on him,
so Hector straight at the doors carried the stone, lifting it,
sentences.i: As a shepherd easily carries the fleece of a ram, taking it up in one hand, and the burden presses on him only a little, so Hector bore the stone straight at the doors, lifting it up,
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘and as when’ opens a simile, and ὣς Ἕκτωρ closes it. ῥεῖα is ‘easily’, πόκον ‘fleece’, and ἄρσενος οἰός ‘of a male sheep’ (ὄϊς, genitive). χειρὶ … ἑτέρῃ is literally ‘with the other hand’, which means one hand, the other being free. μιν is the shepherd; ἐπείγει is ‘presses’. ἰθύς is ‘straight’, here with the genitive σανίδων ‘at the doors’ (σανίς is a board; of a door, a leaf). φέρε is the imperfect ‘bore’; ἀείρας ‘lifting’.

sentences.t:
αἵ ῥα πύλας εἴρυντο πύκα στιβαρῶς ἀραρυίας
δικλίδας ὑψηλάς·
sentences.tr:
hai rha pylas eirynto pyka stibarōs araruias
diklidas hypsēlas·
sentences.l:
which guarded the gates, closely and stoutly fitted,
two-leaved and high;
sentences.i: which guarded the gates, closely and stoutly fitted together, two-leaved and high;
sentences.n: αἵ is ‘which’, the doors of the last unit. εἴρυντο is the imperfect of ἐρύομαι ‘guard, protect’ (a different verb from ἐρύω ‘haul’). πύκα is ‘closely’ and στιβαρῶς ‘stoutly’. ἀραρυίας is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit together’, agreeing with πύλας. δικλίδας ‘two-leaved’ means that each gate was made of two doors; ὑψηλάς is ‘high’.

sentences.t:
δοιοὶ δ’ ἔντοσθεν ὀχῆες
εἶχον ἐπημοιβοί, μία δὲ κληῒς ἐπαρήρει.
sentences.tr:
doioi d’ entosthen ochēes
eichon epēmoiboi, mia de klēïs eparērei.
sentences.l:
and two bars on the inside
held them, crossing each other, and one bolt was fitted over them.
sentences.i: and on the inside two bars held them, crossing one another, and a single bolt was fitted over them.
sentences.n: δοιοὶ … ὀχῆες are ‘two bars’ (ὀχεύς is a bar for holding a door); ἔντοσθεν ‘on the inside’. εἶχον is the imperfect ‘held’. ἐπημοιβοί is a rare adjective, ‘crossing one another’ is a guess at it, and the exact arrangement is not known. κληΐς is the bolt, and ἐπαρήρει the pluperfect of ἐπαραρίσκω, ‘was fitted over’, with the sense of an imperfect.

sentences.t:
στῆ δὲ μάλ’ ἐγγὺς ἰών, καὶ ἐρεισάμενος βάλε μέσσας
εὖ διαβάς, ἵνα μή οἱ ἀφαυρότερον βέλος εἴη,
ῥῆξε δ’ ἀπ’ ἀμφοτέρους θαιρούς·
sentences.tr:
stē de mal’ engys iōn, kai ereisamenos bale messas
eu diabas, hina mē hoi aphauroteron belos eiē,
rhēxe d’ ap’ amphoterous thairous·
sentences.i: He went very close and stood there, and bracing himself he struck the doors in the middle, standing well astride so that his missile should not be weaker, and tore away both hinges;
sentences.n: στῆ is the unaugmented aorist ‘stood’ (ἵστημι), and ἰών ‘going’. ἐρεισάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρείδω ‘brace oneself, lean one’s weight’. μέσσας is the feminine accusative plural ‘the middle parts’, agreeing with the doors left unnamed. εὖ διαβάς ‘well astride’, the aorist participle of διαβαίνω. ἵνα μή οἱ … εἴη is a negative purpose clause with the optative; ἀφαυρότερον is ‘weaker’, and βέλος the missile, the stone. ῥῆξε … ἀπ’ is tmesis, ‘broke off’. θαιρούς are the hinges (a rare word, taken as the pivots on which the doors turn).

sentences.t:
πέσε δὲ λίθος εἴσω
βριθοσύνῃ, μέγα δ’ ἀμφὶ πύλαι μύκον, οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ὀχῆες
ἐσχεθέτην, σανίδες δὲ διέτμαγεν ἄλλυδις ἄλλη
λᾶος ὑπὸ ῥιπῆς·
sentences.tr:
pese de lithos eisō
brithosynēi, mega d’ amphi pylai mykon, oud’ ar’ ochēes
eschethetēn, sanides de dietmagen allydis allē
laos hypo rhipēs·
sentences.l:
and the stone fell inside
by its weight, and loudly around the gates bellowed, and the bars
did not hold, and the doors burst apart, one this way, one that,
under the stone’s rush;
sentences.i: and the stone fell inside by its weight, and the gates bellowed loudly all around, and the bars did not hold, and the doors burst apart, one this way and one that, under the rush of the stone;
sentences.n: βριθοσύνῃ is the dative ‘by weight’ (βρίθω ‘be heavy’). μύκον is the aorist of μυκάομαι ‘bellow’, said of the gates; ἀμφί is an adverb ‘round about’. ἐσχεθέτην is the dual aorist of ἔχω, ‘held (out)’, agreeing with the dual sense of ὀχῆες ‘two bars’. διέτμαγεν is the aorist passive of διατμήγω, ‘burst apart’, with ἄλλυδις ἄλλη ‘this way, that way’. λᾶος is the genitive of λᾶας ‘stone’, and ῥιπῆς the genitive of ῥιπή ‘rush, force of a throw’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔσθορε φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
νυκτὶ θοῇ ἀτάλαντος ὑπώπια·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ar’ esthore phaidimos Hektōr
nykti thoēi atalantos hypōpia·
sentences.l:
and he leapt in, glorious Hector,
the equal of swift night in his looks;
sentences.i: and glorious Hector leapt in, the equal of swift night in his looks;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and he’. ἔσθορε is the aorist of θρῴσκω ‘leap’, with ἐσ- ‘in’. φαίδιμος is the stock ‘glorious’. νυκτὶ θοῇ ἀτάλαντος is ‘equal to swift night’, ἀτάλαντος being ‘equal’ with the dative (the stock phrase is ‘the equal of Ares’). ὑπώπια is an accusative of respect: ὑπώπιον is the part under the eyes, so ‘in the face, in his looks’; the likeness is to the darkness of night.

sentences.t:
λάμπε δὲ χαλκῷ
σμερδαλέῳ, τὸν ἕεστο περὶ χροΐ, δοιὰ δὲ χερσὶ
δοῦρ’ ἔχεν·
sentences.tr:
lampe de chalkōi
smerdaleōi, ton heesto peri chroï, doia de chersi
dour’ echen·
sentences.i: and he shone with frightful bronze, which he wore on his body, and held two spears in his hands;
sentences.n: λάμπε is the imperfect of λάμπω ‘shine’, with χαλκῷ σμερδαλέῳ ‘frightful bronze’ (his armour). τόν is ‘which’; ἕεστο is the pluperfect of ἕννυμι, ‘had put on, wore’; περὶ χροΐ is ‘about the skin’, dative of χρώς. δοιά is ‘two’, with δοῦρ’ (δοῦρα, neuter plural of δόρυ ‘spear’), and ἔχεν is the imperfect ‘held’.

sentences.t:
οὔ κέν τίς μιν ἐρύκακεν ἀντιβολήσας
νόσφι θεῶν ὅτ’ ἐσᾶλτο πύλας·
sentences.tr:
ou ken tis min erykaken antibolēsas
nosphi theōn hot’ esalto pylas·
sentences.l:
no one could have held him back, meeting him,
except gods, when he leapt in at the gates;
sentences.i: no one who met him could have held him back, except the gods, when he leapt in at the gates;
sentences.n: οὔ κέν τίς … ἐρύκακεν is ‘no one could have held back’: κεν with an aorist for what would have happened. ἐρύκακεν is the reduplicated aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’. ἀντιβολήσας is the aorist participle of ἀντιβολέω ‘meet, encounter’. νόσφι θεῶν is ‘apart from gods’, that is, ‘except gods’. ἐσᾶλτο is the aorist of ἐσάλλομαι, with the accusative πύλας ‘the gates’.

sentences.t: πυρὶ δ’ ὄσσε δεδήει.
sentences.tr: pyri d’ osse dedēei.
sentences.l: and with fire his two eyes were ablaze.
sentences.i: and his eyes blazed with fire.
sentences.n: ὄσσε is the dual ‘two eyes’. δεδήει is the pluperfect of δαίω ‘was ablaze’, as at 12.35, with the sense of an imperfect. πυρί is ‘with fire’.

sentences.t:
κέκλετο δὲ Τρώεσσιν ἑλιξάμενος καθ’ ὅμιλον
τεῖχος ὑπερβαίνειν·
sentences.tr:
kekleto de Trōessin helixamenos kath’ homilon
teichos hyperbainein·
sentences.l:
And he gave orders to the Trojans, turning himself about through the throng,
to go over the wall;
sentences.i: He gave orders to the Trojans, turning round among the throng, to go over the wall;
sentences.n: κέκλετο … ἑλιξάμενος is the phrase of 408, now with the infinitive ὑπερβαίνειν ‘to go over’ giving the order. καθ’ ὅμιλον is ‘through the throng’ (ὅμιλος is a crowd).

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ὀτρύνοντι πίθοντο.
sentences.tr: toi d’ otrynonti pithonto.
sentences.l: and they obeyed him, urging them on.
sentences.i: and they obeyed him as he urged them on.
sentences.n: τοί is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’. ὀτρύνοντι is the dative singular of the participle of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, agreeing with ‘him’ (Hector), left unsaid. πίθοντο is the aorist middle of πείθω, ‘obeyed’, here without augment.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ οἳ μὲν τεῖχος ὑπέρβασαν, οἳ δὲ κατ’ αὐτὰς
ποιητὰς ἐσέχυντο πύλας·
sentences.tr:
autika d’ hoi men teichos hyperbasan, hoi de kat’ autas
poiētas esechynto pylas·
sentences.l:
And at once some went over the wall, and others, through the very
well-made gates, poured in;
sentences.i: At once some went over the wall, and others poured in through the well-made gates themselves;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν … οἳ δέ is ‘some … others’. ὑπέρβασαν is the aorist of ὑπερβαίνω ‘go over’, in the epic form for ὑπερέβησαν. κατ’ αὐτὰς ποιητὰς … πύλας is ‘through the very gates, well-made’: αὐτάς points to the gates just broken open. ποιητός is ‘well-made’. ἐσέχυντο is the aorist middle of ἐσχέω ‘pour in’.

sentences.t:
Δαναοὶ δὲ φόβηθεν
νῆας ἀνὰ γλαφυράς, ὅμαδος δ’ ἀλίαστος ἐτύχθη.
sentences.tr:
Danaoi de phobēthen
nēas ana glaphyras, homados d’ aliastos etychthē.
sentences.l:
and the Danaans were put to flight
up among the hollow ships, and an uproar, relentless, was made.
sentences.i: and the Danaans fled among the hollow ships, and a relentless uproar arose.
sentences.n: φόβηθεν is the aorist passive of φοβέομαι, ‘were put to flight’ (-θεν for -θησαν). νῆας ἀνὰ γλαφυράς is ‘up along the hollow ships’, ἀνά with the accusative. ὅμαδος is a din or uproar, and ἀλίαστος ‘relentless’ (its origin is uncertain). ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω, ‘was made, came about’.
